messages.subject: Heterogeneity in detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I have a quick question. I have heterogeneity in my detection history for my sites. I have 132 sites with 14 days of survey (using camera traps). For each day, I have a 0 if no deer was detected and a 1 if a deer was detected throughout the day (24 hours). But, when I look at my detection history, some sites have mostly a detection everyday and some as no detection at all. This, I heard, can cause bias in my occupancy estimation. For now, my models estimate a mean detection probability for all my sites but I would like to know if there is a way to account for heterogeneity in detection in my models in R using unmarkedFrameOccu.

Thanks,
Aimie

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Heterogeneity in detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Dear Aimie,

you could use the so-called Royle-Nichols or heterogeneity occupancy model. See also the interesting paper by Dorazio on the relationship between three types of species distribution models and also the two papers by Royle.

Dorazio, R.M., 2007. On the choice of statistical models for estimating occurrence and extinction from animal surveys. Ecology 88, 2773-2782.
Royle, J.A., 2006. Site occupancy model with heterogeneous detection probabilities. Biometrics 62, 97-102.
Royle, J.A., Nichols, J.D., 2003. Estimating abundance from repeated presence-absence data or point counts. Ecology 84, 777-790.

You can view the RN model as a method to estimate abundance from detection/nondetection (a. erroneously k.a. presence/absence) data or as a method to estimate occupancy in the presence of heterogeneity in detection probability that is caused by among-site variation in abundance.

Best regards -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Aimie,

There is probably a reason why there is detection heterogeneity. The Royle-Nichols model is a good model if variation in abundance causes detection heterogeneity. You may have site covariates which may explain detection heterogeneity. Alternatively, you might fit a model with a site random effect. You can't do this in 'unmarked' (I think) but you can fit some models in 'ubms' (https://kenkellner.com/blog/ubms-vignette.html) or JAGS.

Best wishes,
Beni

messages.body_plain:
Hi Christina,

When you have a dynamic occupancy model fit with mb.gof.test( ), the function returns the global chi-square statistic and corresponding P-value. The global chi-square is computed by summing the chi-squares obtained for each season. This is exactly what you have in the output you included in your original message. If you look into the object a little further, you can also get the summary of observed vs predicted frequencies for each season separately. For example, if you stored the result of mb.gof.test( , nsim = 5000) in an object called outGOF, then you can access these season-specific chi-square tables with:

> dd$chisq.table$tables

These tables can help identify the seasons that are associated with the largest chi-square values. That being said, the huge values you are getting for each season suggest strong lack-of-fit. Also note that the second part of your code with the different test statistics you tried are not appropriate for a model based on detections/non-detections. For the chi-square to work with detection/non-detection data, you need to summarize information (e.g., for detection histories, or rows, or columns).

Good luck,

Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

It's probably because your variable is a site covariate (SiteCov), not an observation variable (ObsCov). Observation variables (ObsCov) are those that vary between each sampling event and sometimes for each site. While site variables only vary for each station.
In this case you mention that your csv has 55 rows and I imagine one column per variable, so the error is that you should have a matrix with the same dimensions as your detection/non-detection history matrix.  In the case you had an observation variable, like the moon phase or daily weather conditions, it should have 55 rows and the same number of columns as the sampling events you defined.
I hope it was clear, but if not you can look at this article from Guillera-Arroita 2017 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecog.02445> ,where the definition of the types of covariates is explained very well, and which ones affect each process.

messages.body_plain:
To expand on what Richard said, gdistsamp handles multiple visits to a site/transect within a single season (to allow estimation of availability). distsampOpen handles multiple seasons of data from a site/transect (to allow estimation of transition rates). Right now there is no explicit way in unmarked to handle multiple seasons of data for a site/transect, when you also have multiple visits within each season (i.e., you can't estimate both availability and transition parameters in the same model).
Ken

messages.body_plain:
Ken is right that you can't estimate availability and transition parameters in the same model in unmarked. However, if you don't care about availability per se, and you just want to model temporal dynamics at each site, you could treat each survey occasion as a primary period and then fit the distsampOpen​ model, which is an extension of the Dail-Madsen (Biometrics, 2011) model.  You would need to introduce a 'yearlySiteCov' to describe the time interval between surveys. This could be a continuous variable (eg, the number of days between surveys) or a factor, perhaps with two levels: 'within-year' and 'among-year. If abundance doesn't change much within seasons, you will get estimates of apparent survival that are close to one and recruitment estimates close to zero. Or you could use one of the other parameterizations for the temporal dynamics, but the idea is the same (N should change less within seasons than among seasons). An alternative would be to use the primaryPeriod​ argument when you create the unmarkedFrame​DSO object. This lets you account for the time interval between surveys using the method described in the Biometrics paper.

Richard

messages.subject: New R package "ubms"
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My R package "ubms" is now available on CRAN [1]. The package allows you to fit many of the same models as unmarked, but in a Bayesian framework with Stan [2] instead of with maximum likelihood. "ubms" allows you to specify random effects on model parameters (e.g., a random observer effect) using the syntax from "lme4", and you also get posterior distributions for parameters.

The interface is designed to be almost identical to unmarked for easy switching back and forth, and it uses unmarkedFrames for data input. So, for example, if you fit an occupancy model in unmarked with the following code:

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(...)
fit <- occu(~1~1, data=umf)

You could fit the same model in Stan like this:

fit2 <- stan_occu(~1~1, data=umf)

Currently there are Stan equivalents of the unmarked functions occu, occuRN, occuTTD, pcount, distsamp, and colext. There are also helper functions for prediction, goodness of fit, and extracting posterior distributions of latent parameters like site-level abundance and occupancy (similar to what ranef() does in unmarked).

This is not meant to be a replacement for unmarked. In fact, I would suggest always fitting models in unmarked first, and only using ubms if you specifically need the extra abilities. Also, while I hope to add more models to ubms in the future, it is unlikely that equivalents to certain more complex unmarked functions like gdistsamp(), pcountOpen(), etc., will ever end up in ubms.

If you'd like to see more details, the package website is here [3] and there is an extended demo of the package features here [4]. Feel free to contact me with questions or issues, or submit bug reports on Github [5]. I hope you find the package useful!

Ken

[1] https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ubms/index.html
[2] https://mc-stan.org/
[3] https://kenkellner.com/ubms/
[4] https://kenkellner.com/blog/ubms-vignette.html
[5] https://github.com/kenkellner/ubms/issues

messages.body_plain:
With this setup of the data, it seems to me that observer is analogous to sample occasion (you have two "samples", but instead of being different in time, they are different in observer). So, it looks like you could just model it like you would sample-specific detection probability to see if there are differences between observers.
Here's how I would do it:

# First simulate some data
n = 100 # number of sites
S = 2 # number of samples
D = matrix(0,n,S) # the detection matrix
p1 = .7 # detection prob for Jane
p2 = .5 # detection prob for John
D[,1] <- rbinom(n,1,p1)
D[,2] <- rbinom(n,1,p2)
Obs1 <- rep("Jane",100)
Obs2 <- rep("John",100)
sim.Data <- data.frame(D,Obs1,Obs2)

# Here's the sample dataset similar to what you showed:
head(sim.Data)

# Now get it into unmarked:
y <- sim.Data[1:2]
Observer <- sim.Data[,3:4]
sim.UMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, obsCovs = list(Observer=Observer))
summary(sim.UMF)

#Now you can see if AIC model selection finds an observer effect:
m0 <- occu(~1~1, data=sim.UMF)
m1 <- occu(~Observer~1, data=sim.UMF)

models <- fitList('p(.)psi(.)' = m0,
                  'p(Obs)psi(.)' = m1)
ms <- modSel(models)
ms

# And it does.

Hi Wade-

I think you're making this harder than it needs to be. I gave you the example of two observer names, but you could use more without changing the code at all. Unmarked is seeing the names as factors and handles them appropriately in the analysis. To convince you, I changed my code to make up the simulated data to have 4 observers, each with a different p. Note that I always had 2 names in the first column, and the 2 other names in the second column, but I only did that so that it wouldn't pick the same name twice in one sample. In your real example any observer name could be in the first or second column.

If you run it, you see that unmarked makes Barbara the intercept because it goes alphabetical. Looking at the results of m1 you see that it found Barbara had the highest p, followed by Jane, John, and Fred, respectively. That matches the true values used for simulation nicely.

Try it:

# First simulate some data

S = 2 # number of samples
D = matrix(0,n,S) # the detection matrix

Obsa <- c("Jane", "John") #choose random observers for obs1
Obsb <- c("Barbara", "Fred") #choose random observers for obs2
Obs1 <- sample(Obsa,n, replace=TRUE)
Obs2 <- sample(Obsb,n, replace=TRUE)

pJane = 0.7
pJohn = 0.5
pBarb = 0.8
pFred = 0.4

p1 <- vector(length=length(Obs1))
for(i in 1:length(Obs1)){
  ifelse(Obs1[i]=="Jane", p1[i] <- pJane, p1[i] <- pJohn)
}

p2 <- vector(length=length(Obs2))
for(i in 1:length(Obs2)){
  ifelse(Obs2[i]=="Barbara", p2[i] <- pBarb, p2[i] <- pFred)

}

D[,1] <- rbinom(n,1,p1)
D[,2] <- rbinom(n,1,p2)

sim.Data <- data.frame(D,Obs1,Obs2)

# Here's the sample dataset similar to what you showed:
head(sim.Data)

# Now get it into unmarked:

Observer <- sim.Data[,3:4]

summary(sim.UMF)

m1 <- occu(~Observer~1, data=sim.UMF)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Ettore.

One comment: You have a very small data set with only 11 sites, so probably should not add more than a single site covariate into the occupancy model. But this does not necessary explain your problem.

Perhaps it's a problem of complete separation: that's when in a logistic regression (and the occupancy part of the model is one) some value of a covariate completely separates all 0s and all 1s in the response, then usual maximum likelihood will get infinity.

I think I would explore your data set with a simple logistic regression first: i.e., model the indicator for whether the beast is ever detected over the 21 surveys (= 1) or not (=0). You have 11 values of the response then. That will emphasize to you the sparsity of your data set, but also perhaps lets you better diagnose causes for your problem.

Assuming that the estimates in your model fit are not totally of the mark, I see that p is estimated at plogis(-1.56) = 0.1736466. So, this means that the combined detection probability in your study is 1 - (1-0.1736466)^21 = 0.98. So you won't risk much when you ignore imperfect detection in this case perhaps.

Best regards  -- Marc
